title: India–Israel and New Minilaterals

cards.h: Two stories: one partner and many small clubs
cards.b:
This lesson joins two fast-changing topics. First, India–Israel, now a Special Strategic Partnership. Second, the new minilaterals: small, flexible groups of three or four states, such as the Quad, I2U2 and IMEC.

India has moved from the big multilateral forums of the Cold War to a style where it joins several issue-based coalitions at once. The reason is simple: the UN and the WTO are stuck, while a handful of like-minded countries can act faster.

Examiners ask what minilaterals add, whether they undermine multilateralism, and how they match strategic autonomy.

cards.h: India and Israel: a long, quiet road
cards.b:
India recognised Israel in 1950 but kept the relationship at a low level because of Arab ties and domestic politics. After 1992 ties grew fast, especially in defence.

During the 1999 Kargil war, Israel sent ammunition, drones and laser-guided bomb kits. Since then India has been among Israel's top arms buyers: drones such as Heron, missiles such as Barak-8 (MRSAM, co-developed with DRDO), Spike anti-tank missiles, radars and the SPICE bomb kit.

• Defence and security: arms, co-development, counter-terrorism and cyber cooperation. The Pegasus spyware controversy (2021) raised domestic questions; the Supreme Court set up a committee.
  • Agriculture and water: Centres of Excellence in many Indian states, drip irrigation and desalination.
  • Technology and innovation: the I4F fund, start-ups, research grants.
  • Trade: about $3.6 billion in 2024-25 (excluding most defence), diamonds a major item.
  • People: Indian caregivers and construction workers in Israel; the Bnei Menashe community.

The two states share a worry about terrorism and a sense of being in tough neighbourhoods.

Modi made a two-day state visit to Israel on 25–26 February 2026. The countries upgraded their ties to a Special Strategic Partnership and signed a series of MoUs (reported as 16). Talks on a free trade agreement had started in New Delhi shortly before. The sides also agreed to explore linking UPI with Israel's payments system and to update defence arrangements for joint projects.

Modi spoke of cooperation in the I2U2 and IMEC formats. The visit drew domestic criticism over the Gaza war.

Two days after the visit, on 28 February 2026, the US and Israel struck Iran. Delhi had to manage the new Israel tie in the middle of a regional war. India kept calling for restraint and dialogue.

India also stays committed to a two-state solution and sends aid to Palestinians.

The term was popularised by Moisés Naím in Foreign Policy (2009): 'minilateralism' means bringing together the smallest number of countries needed to make the largest possible impact on a problem.

Bilateral

Two states.

Minilateral

Three to five like-minded states, informal, issue-based, no big treaty or secretariat.

Multilateral

Many states, formal institutions and rules (UN, WTO).

Advantages: speed, flexibility, shared interests. Drawbacks: exclusion of others, weak enforcement, and the risk of replacing universal rules with great-power clubs. India uses them to supplement, not replace, the UN and WTO.

• I2U2 (India, Israel, UAE, US): launched at a virtual leaders' summit on 14 July 2022. Aims: food security, energy, water, space, health, transport. Projects included a food park in Gujarat and a hybrid renewable energy project.
  • IMEC (below).
  • Trilaterals: India–France–UAE, India–France–Australia, India–Japan–Australia (supply chains), Japan–India–Italy, and others.
  • Colombo Security Conclave on Indian Ocean security.

The big difference from alliances: no joint command, no common enemy named, and each member keeps its own ties.

cards.h: IMEC: the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor
cards.b:
Announced at the G20 summit in New Delhi on 9 September 2023 through an MoU among India, the US, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, the EU, France, Germany and Italy.

  • Eastern leg: Indian ports (such as Mundra) to the UAE by sea.
  • Northern leg: rail across the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Jordan to Israel's Haifa port, then by sea to Europe.
  • Plus an electricity cable, a hydrogen pipeline and a data cable.

It was meant as an alternative to China's Belt and Road. But the Gaza war froze the northern link, and Gulf politics and the 2026 Hormuz disruption cast doubt on Gulf hubs. In 2026 President Trump publicly backed IMEC again, and analysts urged a 'Hormuz-proof' version. No new official timetable existed as of late 2026.

Realists see minilaterals as balancing. Liberals see them as steps towards rules. India's explanation is reformed multilateralism: it still presses for UN reform while building flexible coalitions.

Evidence of the limits: I2U2 has met rarely since 2022, the Quad has not held a leaders' summit since September 2024 and IMEC works only on paper. Strategic autonomy means India can join many and be bound by none.

• Prefer projects with money and deadlines (ports, grids, chips) to long communiqués.
  • Keep a seat at both Western and Eurasian tables: BRICS and SCO, Quad and I2U2.
  • Use groupings to pull in capital and technology for Indian manufacturing.
  • Keep Israel ties on interests, with Palestine and the Arab world managed separately.

For the exam, give examples with dates and one clear criticism. A diagram of overlapping groupings around India is worth marks.

"I2U2 and IMEC: assess their significance for India's West Asia policy." (typical)
"Minilateralism is reshaping India's foreign policy. Discuss." (typical)
"Evaluate the India-Israel strategic partnership." (typical)

Structure: (1) concept of minilateralism; (2) examples: Quad, I2U2, IMEC, trilaterals; (3) India–Israel pillars and the 2026 visit; (4) benefits; (5) limits and risks; (6) way forward: deliver projects, keep multilateralism alive.

quiz.q: I2U2 stands for India, Israel, UAE and:
quiz.w: India, Israel, the United Arab Emirates and the United States.

quiz.q: IMEC was announced at which summit?
quiz.w: At the G20 summit in New Delhi, 9 September 2023.
